title: How I Handled Misbehaviors on the First Day of Zoom Classroom
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. narrates how he handled a profanity-laced misbehavior incident on the literal first day of synchronous Zoom instruction at his school. After two students repeatedly flashed their video on and off making faces, one responded to a calm correction with profanity; Stuart removed him from the call, filed a brief report with his principal, and made a point of checking in with the second student during independent work time rather than dwelling on the incident. He explicitly frames his restraint as intentional; with roughly a hundred students on his rosters, he didn't want one incident to consume disproportionate time or emotional energy. The following class period, the disciplined student returned without incident, and the previously reserved co-offending student volunteered twice during discussion, which Stuart reads as evidence the approach worked. He closes by naming the underlying moves explicitly: working to genuinely like a difficult student regardless of how he's treated, starting a 2x10 relationship-building effort, and using the interaction to reinforce both credibility (I care about you) and belonging (people like you belong in this class).
points: Stuart's response to a student's on-camera profanity was calm and proportionate: a brief boundary statement, immediate removal from the Zoom call, and a written report to his principal, with no extended confrontation.

He explicitly avoided over-investing in the single incident, noting Student X is 'one of a hundred or so students' on his rosters, instead redirecting attention to the co-offending student, Y, via a quick one-on-one check-in during independent work time.

The intervention doubles as the start of a 2x10 relationship-building strategy; Stuart frames the goal as communicating credibility (I care) and belonging (people like you belong here) rather than punishment for its own sake.

The payoff is tracked concretely: the disciplined student returned the next class period, and the previously quiet co-offending student volunteered twice in whole-class discussion, 'infinity percent more' than any prior day.
quotes: They were taking turns flashing their videos on and off, making funny faces each time they'd appear. I could tell they were getting a real kick out of it.
I told the student that we don't speak like that to one another, and then I removed him from the Zoom. This was the first day of Zoom class all year.

Hey, do you understand why I can't have you and Student X flashing your videos on and off like that? I'm not trying to pick on you guys, but I do want a place where we can all focus when we're on Zoom together.

I did not want to fall into the trap of placing any more time or effort into this one situation; after all, Student X is one of a hundred or so students on my rosters this semester, and I owe a shot at an education to all of them.

I remember thinking that day, "Well, I really hope Student X is in class tomorrow." I prayed that he would be. And I noted that Student Y volunteered his voice during our whole-class discussion twice.
First, I am working to like Student X — to genuinely value, know, and respect him. I want to like him no matter how he treats me.
A student's treatment of me (and you) is rarely personal, and even when it is, I don't need to take it to heart.
